issues.legal_issue: A pending appeal from a joint decree for pre-emption abates in its entirety when one appellant dies and the deceased appellant’s legal representatives are not brought on record, if the decree cannot be varied for the surviving appellants without creating conflicting decrees.
material_facts: The property was conveyed to multiple purchasers in a single transaction, with the purchasers to enjoy it in equal shares rather than as separate items of property.
A decree for pre-emption was passed against the purchasers, who appealed jointly.
One appellant died while the appeal was pending, and no application was made to bring that appellant’s legal representatives on record.
The decree for pre-emption as to the deceased appellant’s interest had become final by reason of the abatement.
issues.conclusion: The entire appeal abated and was dismissed with costs.
issues.legal_principle: Pre-emption substitutes the pre-emptor for the purchaser, and a partial pre-emption decree is not possible. Where a decree is joint and part of it becomes final through abatement, the entire appeal abates if allowing the remaining appeal would produce conflicting decrees. The Court relied on Jhanda Singh v. Gurmukh Singh.

predicates.appeal_from_joint_preemption_decree: The proceeding is an appeal by purchasers against a decree granting pre-emption.
predicates.appellant_died_without_representatives_a: One appellant died during the appeal and the appellant’s legal representatives were not added to the proceeding.
predicates.purchasers_acquired_property_jointly: The purchasers acquired the property together rather than acquiring distinct, separately conveyed items.
predicates.partial_relief_would_create_conflicting_: Proceeding with the surviving appellants’ appeal would risk inconsistent decrees concerning the same pre-emption claim.

issues.definition: When an appellant dies without representatives being added in an appeal from a joint pre-emption decree, and the purchasers acquired the property jointly or partial relief would create conflicting decrees, the entire appeal abates.

issues.legal_issue: Repeal of an enactment whose definitions and restrictions are incorporated by reference does not extinguish a separate pre-emption enactment that remains in force; the incorporated definition continues to apply, while restrictions dependent on the repealed enactment cease to operate.
material_facts: The pre-emption enactment defined agricultural land by reference to a separate enactment and also referred to that enactment in provisions restricting who could claim pre-emption and when a decree could be granted.
The separate enactment was repealed, but the pre-emption enactment was not repealed.
The land in the claim met the definition incorporated by reference.
issues.conclusion: The incorporated definition continued to govern the meaning of agricultural land, while the restrictions dependent on the repealed enactment ceased to operate; repeal did not make the substantive pre-emption right unavailable to persons who met its terms.
issues.legal_principle: Where provisions of one enactment are incorporated by reference into another, repeal of the former generally does not affect the incorporated provisions in the latter. The Court relied on Clark v. Bradlaugh. It further held that removal of restrictions did not nullify the substantive pre-emption provision.

rule.if: statutory_preemption_claim and external_definition_incorporated and source_enactment_repealed and preemption_enactment_remained_in_force

predicates.statutory_preemption_claim: A claimant seeks pre-emption under a statutory enactment that remains in force.
predicates.external_definition_incorporated: The continuing enactment incorporates a definition from another enactment by reference.
predicates.source_enactment_repealed: The enactment supplying the incorporated definition or restrictions has been repealed.
predicates.preemption_enactment_remained_in_force: The enactment creating the substantive pre-emption right was not itself repealed.

issues.definition: If a continuing statutory pre-emption claim uses an incorporated definition from a repealed enactment, the right remains available with that definition and without restrictions that depended on the repealed enactment.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory pre-emption right confined to near family members who would inherit the property is a reasonable restriction on free alienation in the interest of the general public.
material_facts: The property was agricultural land sold by its owner.
The claimant asserted a right to pre-empt as the vendor’s son or another close family member entitled to succeed to the property under the applicable order of succession.
The statutory right was confined to members of the vendor’s family who would have been entitled to inherit, and the claim was challenged as an unreasonable restriction on property rights.
issues.conclusion: The pre-emption provision, both as originally framed and in its amended form, was a reasonable restriction in the interest of the general public and did not violate the constitutional protection of property rights.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(5) of the Constitution, the restriction was justified by the purposes of preserving village and community integrity and, independently, allowing the next in succession a chance to retain family property. The Court relied on Bhau Ram v. Baij Nath and Uttam Singh v. Kartar Singh, and distinguished a right granted broadly to relatives from one confined to likely heirs.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_family_preem: A party challenges the constitutionality of a statutory pre-emption right based on the claimant’s family relationship to the vendor.
predicates.claimant_is_near_family_successor: The claimant is a close family member who would be entitled to succeed to the vendor’s property under the applicable succession order.
predicates.statutory_right_limited_to_family_succes: The statutory pre-emption right is confined to family members who would succeed to the property rather than extended broadly to relatives.
predicates.restriction_serves_village_cohesion_or_f: The restriction is directed at preserving village-community cohesion or giving likely family successors a chance to retain family property.

issues.definition: A challenged family-based pre-emption restriction is reasonable in the general public interest when the claimant is a near family successor, the right is limited to family successors, and the restriction serves village cohesion or family-property retention.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-emption right in favour of an owner within an assessed land unit is a reasonable restriction on the vendor’s right to alienate property when owners in that unit share liability for its land revenue.
material_facts: The claimant owned land within an estate, while the purchaser did not own land there.
The estate was an assessment unit, and its landowners were jointly and severally liable for the land revenue assessed on it.
The purchaser challenged the pre-emption right as an unreasonable restriction on property rights.
issues.conclusion: The restriction on the vendor’s right was reasonable and was not repugnant to the constitutional protection of property rights.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the shared liability of landowners within an estate as making the claimant’s position akin to that of a co-sharer, and held the resulting restriction reasonable. It relied on Bhau Ram v. Baij Nath.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_estate_owner: A party challenges the constitutionality of a pre-emption right based on ownership within an assessed land unit.
predicates.claimant_owns_land_in_assessed_unit: The claimant owns land within the same assessed unit as the property being sold.
predicates.owners_share_revenue_liability: Owners within the assessed unit are jointly liable for the land revenue assessed on that unit.

issues.definition: A challenged pre-emption restriction based on ownership in an assessed unit is reasonable when the claimant owns land there and its owners share revenue liability.

issues.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment barring decrees inconsistent with its substantive pre-emption provisions applies in a pending appeal, including an appeal from a decree that granted pre-emption under the former law.
material_facts: A claimant obtained a trial decree for pre-emption under a statutory category that gave a right to owners within an estate.

While the case was on appeal, an amendment removed that category and provided that no decree inconsistent with the amended enactment could be passed in suits instituted before or after its commencement.
The appeal remained pending when the amendment took effect.
issues.conclusion: The amended substantive law applied to the pending appeal; the pre-emption decree was set aside and the suit was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The amendment’s language was comprehensive and retrospective, requiring appellate courts to apply its substantive provisions whether the appeal was from a decree granting or refusing pre-emption. An appeal is a rehearing, and the trial decree does not retain finality while the appeal is pending. The Court relied on Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri and approved Ram Lal v. Raja Ram.

rule.if: pending_preemption_appeal and amendment_covers_preexisting_suits and amendment_removed_basis_for_claim and decree_conflicts_with_amended_law

predicates.pending_preemption_appeal: An appeal concerning a pre-emption claim remains pending when the governing law changes.
predicates.amendment_covers_preexisting_suits: The amendment expressly applies to suits instituted before as well as after it takes effect.
predicates.amendment_removed_basis_for_claim: The amendment removes the statutory category on which the claimant relied for pre-emption.
predicates.decree_conflicts_with_amended_law: The existing decree grants relief that the amended substantive law no longer permits.

issues.definition: When an amendment applies to pre-existing suits, removes the basis for a claim, and makes the existing decree impermissible, a pending pre-emption appeal results in the decree being set aside and the claim being dismissed.
